processes: Counting shells from the period number
Stepping across from metals to nonmetals
Linking row position to atom size
plainLanguageExplanation: A period is a horizontal row of the periodic table. The table is laid out in rows and columns, and the rows are the periods. The period number tells you how many electron shells the elements in that row have: elements in period 1 have one shell, period 2 elements have two shells, and so on. That is why hydrogen and helium, the two elements with just one shell, sit in the very first row. As you move left to right across a period, something interesting happens: the elements gradually change character. The left side of a row holds the metals — shiny, conductive, reactive elements like sodium and magnesium. The middle holds the metalloids, which are in between. And the right side of the row holds the nonmetals — like oxygen and fluorine — which are poor conductors and behave quite differently. So a period is not just a row: it is a complete journey across the personality of the elements, from metal to nonmetal.

whyItMatters: The period tells you how many shells an atom has and lets you trace the great metal-to-nonmetal shift across the table. Reading periods along with groups lets you locate any element and predict its basic character — whether it behaves as a metal, a metalloid, or a nonmetal — straight from its position on the table.
tagline: The table's rows of shell counts
didYouKnow: Every element in period 3 — from sodium to argon — has exactly three electron shells, even though their personalities range from explosive metal to sleepy gas.
compareReason: Rows and columns are the two axes of the periodic table — comparing a period with a group makes clear that rows count shells while columns share behavior.
